newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-KJUS EMERGES AS COMBINED FAVOURITE.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-KJUS EMERGES AS COMBINED FAVOURITE.

text.p: Olympic champion Lasse Kjus emerged as the favourite for the men's combined title at the Alpine skiing world championships on Thursday.

The Norwegian, who won the world title in 1993 and then finished runner-up in the event at the 1996 championships behind Marc Girardelli of Luxembourg, posted the third fastest time over the first leg of a floodlit slalom.

That, combined with the third fastest time in the afternoon's downhill, left him 0.13 seconds ahead of second placed Swiss Bruno Kernen -- whose surprising result could yet bring his country their first world title in four years.
The top two had the same time in the downhill but Kjus clocked 47.38 in the first leg to Kernen's 47.51.
Norwegian Kjetil-Andre Aamodt, the 1993 combined silver medallist and a former double world champion in the technical disciplines, was in third place, 0.37 behind Kjus.
Girardelli, who has not competed since December due to injury, is not defending his title.
Aamodt had been second fastest in the downhill but lost ground after only the 10th fastest slalom leg.
The two race combined event is a simple addition of the downhill and slalom times without handicaps.
The second leg was due to begin at 2000 GMT.
Austrian speed specialist Werner Franz led after the downhill on the Kandahar Banchetta course but came to grief as many had expected on the nearby slalom piste.

If Kjus, who won a World Cup combined last month, hangs on in the second leg of the slalom to take the gold, he will be Norway's second champion in two men's races in Sestriere and will also pick up his second medal.
Atle Skaardal won the gold in last Monday's super-G, ahead of Kjus who settled for the silver, signalling his return to form after a long absence due to sickness.

Austria's big hope, Guenther Mader, who has four world championship combined bronze medals, was lying in fourth place a second behind Kjus. Compatriot Christian Mayer was in fifth place, 1.25 seconds off the pace.
